'''Sylvia Olga Fedoruk''' ([Fe-doruk]; Ukrainian: Федорук) {{post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|SOM}} (May 5, 1927 – September 26, 2012) was a [[Canadians|Canadian]] physicist, [[medical physicist]], curler and the 17th [[lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan]], from 1988 to 1994.

==Life==
Born in [[Canora, Saskatchewan]] to [[Ukrainian Canadian#Settlement – First wave (1891–1914)|Ukrainian immigrants]] Annie Romaniuk and Theodore Fedoruk, Fedoruk attended a [[one room schoolhouse]] in [[Wroxton, Saskatchewan|Wroxton]], north east of [[Yorkton]]. Her father was her teacher.

During World War II, her family relocated to Ontario where her parents took war factory work. In 1946, Fedoruk completed her studies at [[Walkerville Collegiate]] in [[Windsor, Ontario|Windsor Ontario]], at the top of her class and was awarded the Ernest J. Creed Memorial Medal and an entrance [[scholarship]] to attend [[University]]. However, the family chose to return to Saskatchewan where Sylvia entered the University of Saskatchewan at Saskatoon in the fall of 1946.

She received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in physics, at the [[University of Saskatchewan]], in 1949 and was awarded the [[Governor General's Gold Medal]]. Fedoruk then went on to complete her [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] in physics in 1951.

Fedoruk was recruited by Dr. [[Harold E. Johns]] to be the [[Medical Physicist|radiation physicist]] at Saskatoon Cancer Clinic. She became the chief [[medical physicist]] at the [[Saskatoon, Saskatchewan|Saskatoon]] Cancer Clinic and director of physics services at the Saskatchewan Cancer Clinic. She was a [[professor]] of [[oncology]] and associate member in [[physics]] at the University of Saskatchewan. She was involved in the development of the world's first [[cobalt-60]] unit and one of the first [[nuclear medicine]] scanning machines. The cobalt-60 beam therapy unit, or the "cobalt bomb" as it was known, was the first of its kind to successfully use targeted radiation to treat cancer in a patient. The machine's collimated beam of radiation could be adjusted to the size of the tumor to irradiate the growth. Fedoruk's masters work on depth-dose measurements for radiation treatment were essential in the success of the beam therapy unit.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Building on a legacy of nuclear medicine excellence |url=https://canada150.usask.ca/discoveries-with-impact/building-on-a-legacy-of-nuclear-medicine-excellence.php |access-date=February 11, 2021 |website=Canada 150 @ usask |language=en}}</ref>

In 1961, she played the third for [[Joyce McKee]] for the Saskatchewan [[curling]] team, the winners in the very first [[Scotties Tournament of Hearts|Diamond 'D' Championships.]]The next year team Saskatchewan was a runner-up in the [[1962 Diamond D Championship]] with Fedoruk again playing as third. From 1971 to 1972 she was president of the Canadian Ladies [[Curling]] Association. In 1986, she was inducted into the  [[Canadian Curling Hall of Fame]],<ref name="cdnmedhall2">{{Cite web |title=The Honourable Sylvia Fedoruk |url=https://www.cdnmedhall.org/inductees/sylviafedoruk |accessdate=April 20, 2021 |publisher=[[Canadian Medical Hall of Fame]]}}</ref> as a builder,<ref>{{cite web |title=Fedoruk, Hon. Sylvia — CCA Hall of Fame — ACC Temple de la Renommée Virtuelle |url=https://www.curling.ca/hof/people/fedoruk-hon-sylvia-syl/ |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101063406/https://www.curling.ca/hof/people/fedoruk-hon-sylvia-syl/ |archivedate=January 1, 2018}}</ref> and was awarded the [[Saskatchewan Order of Merit]].

From 1986 to 1989 she was chancellor of the University of Saskatchewan. She was the first woman to fill this position at the University of Saskatchewan<ref>{{Cite web |title=Deo et Patriae: Events in the History of the University of Saskatchewan: 1986 |url=http://scaa.usask.ca/gallery/uofs_events/articles/1986.php |website=scaa.usask.ca}}</ref> and was the first woman member of the [[CNSC|Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada]]. Then in 1987, she was made an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Government of Canada — Office of the Secretary to the Governor General — Information and Media Services |title=Order of Canada |url=http://archive.gg.ca/honours/search-recherche/honours-desc.asp?lang=e&TypeID=orc&id=518 |website=archive.gg.ca}}</ref>

From 1988 to 1994, she was [[Lieutenant Governor of Saskatchewan]].

In the 1990s, the City of [[Saskatoon, Saskatchewan|Saskatoon]] named a new road, Fedoruk Drive in her honour. The roadway runs from Central Avenue to McOrmond Drive, north of the communities of Silverspring and Evergreen and south of the community of Aspen Ridge and the Northeast Swale. Fedoruk Drive serves as a minor arterial roadway in the northeast sector of the city.

On October 3, 2012, the name of the Canadian Centre for Nuclear Innovation (CCNI) was changed to the [[Sylvia Fedoruk Canadian Centre for Nuclear Innovation]] in honor of the pioneering work she did in the treatment of cancer using cobalt-60 radiation therapy in the 1950s.<ref>{{Cite journal |year=2012 |title=U of S nuclear centre to be named for Fedoruk |journal=[[The StarPhoenix]]}}</ref>

In 2009, she was inducted into the [[Canadian Medical Hall of Fame]].<ref name="cmhf2">{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |year= |title=The Honourable Sylvia Fedoruk |url=https://www.cdnmedhall.org/inductees/sylviafedoruk |access-date=February 10, 2021 |website=Canadian Medical Hall of Fame}}</ref>
